title: Etiquette
intro: 1. Don't tip — Tipping is not customary and can embarrass service staff; exception: tour guides and porters (¥20–50/day acceptable and appreciated for guides); 5-star hotel staff follow international norms and won't refuse tips 2. Greet with a nod or slight bow — Handshakes are acceptable at business settings; a respectful nod is sufficient for everyday interactions; no hugging strangers 3. Two hands for business cards/gifts — Present and receive with both hands; this is a mark of respect; inspect what you receive before putting it away 4. Be direct about food/drink preferences — Chinese hosts take pride in hospitality through food; politely declining requires firmness: "我吃饱了" (Wǒ chī bǎo le = I'm full); declining multiple times is expected before acceptance 5. No photos inside government buildings and many temples — Look for 禁止拍照 (no photography) signs; always ask at temples; the Forbidden City outer areas are fine, inner galleries sometimes not 6. Dress modestly at temples — Shoulders and knees covered at Buddhist/Taoist temples; the White Cloud Temple (Taoist) is stricter than tourist-oriented Buddhist temples 7. Avoid public displays of affection in conservative areas — Fine in Sanlitun or near 5-star hotels; less appropriate near temples or older neighborhoods 8. Don't point with your finger — Use an open hand to gesture; pointing at people with index finger is rude 9. Bargaining is expected in markets but not in shops/malls — Silk Street and Wangfujing markets: bargain (start at 20–30% of asking price); any mall or restaurant: fixed price 10. Loudness in restaurants is normal — Noise is not rudeness in Chinese restaurant culture; don't be surprised or alarmed; it's a sign of a lively meal

bullets.heading: CHINA — BEIJING
items: Avoid: Clock as a gift (钟 zhōng sounds like 终 zhōng = "end/death"); green hats (associated with infidelity)
Avoid: Sticking chopsticks upright in rice (resembles incense sticks at funeral offerings)
Avoid: Talking about Taiwan as a country, Tibet independence — never raise in conversation
OK sign (circle with thumb and index): Acceptable
Waving "no": Shake hand side to side (not index finger wagging like in West)
Shop at independent hutong artisan shops over tourist market stalls (better quality, more of the money stays local)
Eat at locally-recommended spots rather than tourist restaurants near Tiananmen
Use DiDi over ride-hailing services that exploit drivers; tip your local guide

bullets.heading: VIETNAM — ALL CITIES
items: Avoid: Pointing with index finger (use open hand); crossing fingers in photos (symbolizes the female genitalia in Vietnam — locals will react); showing the bottom of your feet to someone (insulting)
Avoid: Snapping fingers to get a server's attention (rude); instead, make eye contact and give a slight nod
Wai (hands clasped in prayer): Acceptable greeting at temples; not necessary in everyday settings
Stay at locally-owned boutique hotels in Hội An (not just the Đà Nẵng mega-resorts) for one night if possible
Buy directly from artisans at Kim Bong and Thanh Ha villages (see 12-hidden-gems)
Order Vietnamese coffee at local shops, not Highlands Coffee (chain)
Tip your Grab drivers — they're gig workers earning very little per ride

10–15% at restaurants with table service; round up at street stalls; tip tour guides and drivers ($1–2/person/day); nothing is expected but everything is appreciated
Always look for a pile of shoes; follow the lead of locals entering
Dress modestly at temples and pagodas
Sarongs often available to borrow at temple entrances if you forget; tank tops alone are not sufficient
Don't touch the heads of adults or children
In Vietnamese (and broadly Buddhist) culture, the head is sacred
